name: Prompting vs Fine-Tuning vs RAG
intent: Choose between changing the instructions, supplying documents at question time, or changing the model's weights, and know what each one can and cannot fix.
scenario: A legal team wants an assistant that answers from its own policy documents, writes in the firm's house style and returns answers in a fixed format. Three people propose three different fixes: a better prompt, a retrieval system and a fine-tuned model.
problem: When a model's answers are not good enough, there are three levers, and they change different things. Picking the wrong one is expensive: fine-tuning a model to teach it facts that change every month, or building a retrieval system to fix a formatting problem that an example in the prompt would have solved. The levers are not rivals either, as most real systems use more than one.

howItWorks.title: Prompting changes the instructions
howItWorks.text: Instructions, a role and a few worked examples go into the prompt with every request. The GPT-3 paper showed that a large model can pick up a task from demonstrations given purely as text, with no change to its weights. A prompt takes minutes to change and costs nothing to roll back, but it uses part of the context window on every call.

howItWorks.title: Retrieval changes what the model can see
howItWorks.text: Retrieval-augmented generation fetches the relevant passages at question time and puts them in the prompt. The RAG paper describes the model's weights as its parametric memory and the document index as a non-parametric memory that can be swapped to update knowledge as the world changes. It suits facts that are private, large or changing.

howItWorks.title: Fine-tuning changes the weights
howItWorks.text: Training the model further on examples changes how it behaves: a consistent style, a strict format, a specialised skill, a short prompt that works because the habit is built in. It needs good examples, a training run and a fresh evaluation, and the result is a snapshot that does not follow your documents as they change.

howItWorks.title: Match the lever to the problem
howItWorks.text: Missing or changing knowledge points to retrieval. A format, tone or reasoning habit points to prompting first and fine-tuning if it must hold across a high volume of requests. A task the base model cannot do at all may call for a different model or for fine-tuning with a lot of examples.

howItWorks.title: Start with the cheapest and measure
howItWorks.text: A common order is prompting, then retrieval, then fine-tuning, moving on only when a measured gap remains. Build a small evaluation set first, so that each step shows whether it helped. Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA cut the cost of fine-tuning: in the LoRA paper's GPT-3 experiments the trainable parameters fell by 10,000 times and the hardware needed by 3 times, compared with full fine-tuning.

howItWorks.title: Combine them
howItWorks.text: A typical system uses a prompt for instructions and format, retrieval for facts, and sometimes a fine-tuned model to make the prompt shorter or the style steadier. Each part can be improved and tested separately.

pros: Prompting is instant to change and easy to roll back
Retrieval keeps answers current and lets the user check the source documents
Fine-tuning can make behaviour consistent and let a smaller, cheaper model do a narrow job
Each lever can be tested on its own against the same evaluation set
cons: Prompts grow long and costly, and can be fragile when the wording changes
Retrieval adds a system to build and tune, and can fetch the wrong passages
Fine-tuning needs data, training, evaluation and a repeat when the base model changes
Combining all three adds parts that can each fail
whenToUse: You are deciding how to fix a gap between what a model does and what you need
A new feature needs private or frequently changing knowledge
You need consistent style, format or tone at high volume
whenNotToUse: Do not fine-tune to add facts that change: retrieval keeps them current
Do not build retrieval to fix a format or tone problem that examples in the prompt can solve
Do not choose a lever before you have an evaluation set that shows the gap
pitfalls: Fine-tuning on a small set of examples that covers only part of the cases, and losing general ability
Assuming that fine-tuned knowledge is reliable: a model can still state it wrongly
Retrieving too many passages, so that the useful ones are lost in the middle of a long prompt
Tuning the prompt on a handful of cases and calling it fixed without a test set

quiz.question: A team wants an assistant that answers from its policy documents, and the policies change every week. What should they try first?
options: Fine-tune a model on the current policies, and repeat the training run each week
Retrieve the relevant policy passages at question time and put them in the prompt
Write the whole policy manual into the system prompt and never change the model
Wait for a new base model that has the latest policies in its training data
quiz.explanation: Facts that change are best supplied at question time, so that updating a document updates the answers at once. Weekly fine-tuning is slow and costly and still not a reliable way to store facts. A whole manual in every prompt is costly and may not fit, and a future base model will not contain your private policies.

quiz.question: A model gives correct answers but breaks the required output format in about 20 percent of calls, even with examples in the prompt. The company has thousands of correctly formatted examples and a high request volume. What is a reasonable next step?
options: Add a retrieval system, since format errors are caused by a lack of context
Raise the temperature, so that the model explores more formats and finds the right one
Remove the examples from the prompt, because examples confuse the model about the format
Use structured output or validation first, and fine-tune on the correct examples if the gap remains
quiz.explanation: A format problem is about behaviour, not missing knowledge. Structured output and validation are cheap fixes to try, and with plenty of good examples and high volume, fine-tuning is a sound way to make the format reliable. Retrieval, higher temperature and removing examples do not address it.

quiz.question: A team fine-tunes a model on its product manual, hoping that it will then quote current prices. The prices change every month. What is the problem with this plan?
options: Facts baked into weights go stale and are not reliably recalled, so prices are better supplied by retrieval
Fine-tuning can only change the style of answers, so the model would not learn anything from the manual
Prices cannot be written as text, so a language model cannot be trained on them
The model would learn the prices perfectly, but the training run would take longer than a month
quiz.explanation: Fine-tuning shapes behaviour, and a model can still state trained-in facts wrongly, and they are out of date after the next change. Retrieval from a current price list is the right tool. Fine-tuning does change more than style, and prices are plain text, and the problem is staleness, not training time.
